_readme: Radio script. tag: 'story' for the 4052 fiction, 'real' for NASA facts (each real line matches a fact on a card or in CLAUDE.md). Keep lines short (ages 10-14).

intro.text: Recovery Traveler, do you read me? This is Mission Control. The year is 4052.
Earth is still home, but it's weaker than it used to be. Its shield is failing, and asteroids keep coming.
Your job: find the machines humans sent into space between the 1960s and 2026, and scan them into the Archive.
We don't take them. We scan a hologram copy and leave each original where it rests, as a monument.
Most of them went quiet long ago. Nobody visits them. That's why they need you: so they're not forgotten.
You won't be alone. The Numans, a life form we met not long ago, have offered to help. They're the reason people can live on Mars.
We sing frequencies that shatter stone. But our songs need a human partner to keep time.
So here's the deal: play their rhythm games. Every song you clear protects Earth and unlocks a machine to scan.
Left lane is A or the left arrow. Right lane is D or the right arrow. You can tap the lanes too.
Start on the Moon to learn the rhythm, or jump straight to Mars. Good luck, Traveler.

moon.text: Moon approach. This is where people first walked on another world.
Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969. The bottom half of its lander is still sitting there.
Apollo 17's rover is parked in the Taurus-Littrow valley. It drove 30.5 kilometers on batteries.
Your Moon is quiet. But it remembers every machine that touched it. We can hear them, very faintly.
The Moon songs are gentle. Learn the rhythm here, Traveler.

mars.text: Mars. In 1976, Viking 1 became the first US spacecraft to land here and send back pictures.
Opportunity was built for 90 Martian days. It kept going for almost 15 years.
Mars is our home now too. We helped make it livable for your people. These machines were here first.
Two rovers from your time, Curiosity and Perseverance, are on our friends list, not our scan list.
Listen for the data break. When the beat drops out, you're hearing real mission data. Play its peaks.

deep.text: Deep space. Out here, distance is everything.
Voyager 1 launched in 1977. It's almost one light-day from Earth, so a message takes nearly a whole day to reach it.
Cassini ended its mission on purpose, diving into Saturn to keep moons like Enceladus clean for future explorers.
These are the loneliest songs. Some of these machines are still listening. Play loud.
Fast songs ahead, Traveler. Earth is counting on you.

great.text: That's a clean scan! The Numans are humming along.
Perfect timing. The shield lit up all the way across the sky.
You keep time like a star keeps light. We are impressed.

ok.text: Signal locked. Not perfect, but the machine is safe in the Archive.
Good enough to scan! The shield is holding.
A little wobbly. We liked it anyway.

fail.text: We lost the signal. Shake it off and try again.
So close! The machine isn't going anywhere. It has waited for decades.
Same song, again. Your timing is getting better. We can hear it.

scanned.text: Archive confirms: {short} is scanned. The original stays at {place}, right where it was left.

lines.text: The Archive is a museum on Earth. Every machine you scan becomes a full-size hologram there.
Kids walk under Voyager's dish and sit next to the Apollo rover. Nobody is allowed to touch the real ones.
The shield is a web of light around Earth that turns space rocks away. It is very old now.
Every Numan song you finish patches a few holes. That's why the radar on your dash never stops beeping.
Nobody knows exactly where the Numans came from. They talk in frequencies and glow when they're happy.
They think human music is the funniest thing in the universe. They also think it's beautiful. Both at once.
This recovery ship has carried twelve travelers before you. Someone left a coffee mug. Someone left a plant.
Somebody wrote 'Feed the Numans?' on the checklist. Nobody knows if Numans eat.
In 4052, every landing site is a protected place. We look. We scan. We don't touch.
The machines are real, and so are their stories. Every fact on their cards comes from NASA.
